L4.title: SPORT COMPETITION IN SCHOOL
L4.title_vi: Cuộc thi thể thao ở trường
L4.script_text: People often have quick opinions about sport competition in school, but my experience has been more complicated. At first I expected the most obvious explanation to be right, and I even considered the idea that they usually have positive effects on students. Another possibility people often mention is that they help students avoid physical risks. After looking at the situation more carefully, neither description really matched what happened. The better summary is that things were negative effects. That difference matters because the speaker's final judgement is more qualified than the tempting alternatives. There is another aspect that is easy to miss. Some people argue that it makes students' lives more unbalanced, while others go almost to the opposite extreme and say that it leaves little time for other activities. My own view sits elsewhere. What matters is creates balance. In other words, the conclusion depends on the exact conditions being discussed, not on a broad slogan. During the discussion I might use several words related to the wrong choices, because they are realistic possibilities. That does not make them the answer. The key is to notice when an idea is introduced only to be limited, corrected, or rejected. Expressions such as “however”, “in practice”, “actually”, and “what matters more” often signal that the speaker is moving toward the real position. For a listening task, I would therefore avoid selecting an option as soon as I hear familiar vocabulary. I would wait until the evaluation becomes clear, then match that meaning to the option that paraphrases it most accurately. The two ideas to retain from this talk are the ones expressed through negative effects, damaging and creates balance, student life; they represent the settled view rather than the rejected alternatives. A longer talk also includes background that may not directly answer either question. For example, a speaker may describe how the issue developed, mention another person's view, or give a small personal example before returning to the main judgement. Those details are useful context, but they should not replace the two target conclusions. When I practise, I try to separate background information from evaluation language. Background tells me what happened; evaluation tells me what the speaker finally thinks about it. I also listen for changes in certainty. Words such as 'probably', 'only', 'not always', 'unlikely', and 'depends' can completely change which option is accurate. If two answers share similar vocabulary, the safer choice is the one that matches the strength and direction of the speaker's final judgement.

options: They usually have positive effects on students.
They help students avoid physical risks.

L4.title: TELEVISION SERIES
L4.script_text: People often have quick opinions about television series, but my experience has been more complicated. At first I expected the most obvious explanation to be right, and I even considered the idea that its quality changes considerably from one episode to another. Another possibility people often mention is that some episodes are much weaker than the others. After looking at the situation more carefully, neither description really matched what happened. The better summary is that things were steady. That difference matters because the speaker's final judgement is more qualified than the tempting alternatives. There is another aspect that is easy to miss. Some people argue that the series is made without considering its audience, while others go almost to the opposite extreme and say that viewer preferences have little effect on production decisions. My own view sits elsewhere. What matters is audience. In other words, the conclusion depends on the exact conditions being discussed, not on a broad slogan. During the discussion I might use several words related to the wrong choices, because they are realistic possibilities. That does not make them the answer. The key is to notice when an idea is introduced only to be limited, corrected, or rejected. Expressions such as “however”, “in practice”, “actually”, and “what matters more” often signal that the speaker is moving toward the real position. For a listening task, I would therefore avoid selecting an option as soon as I hear familiar vocabulary. I would wait until the evaluation becomes clear, then match that meaning to the option that paraphrases it most accurately. The two ideas to retain from this talk are the ones expressed through steady, standard and audience, viewing habits; they represent the settled view rather than the rejected alternatives. A longer talk also includes background that may not directly answer either question. For example, a speaker may describe how the issue developed, mention another person's view, or give a small personal example before returning to the main judgement. Those details are useful context, but they should not replace the two target conclusions. When I practise, I try to separate background information from evaluation language. Background tells me what happened; evaluation tells me what the speaker finally thinks about it. I also listen for changes in certainty. Words such as 'probably', 'only', 'not always', 'unlikely', and 'depends' can completely change which option is accurate. If two answers share similar vocabulary, the safer choice is the one that matches the strength and direction of the speaker's final judgement.

options: It has the consistent quality throughout
Its quality changes considerably from one episode to another.
Some episodes are much weaker than the others.
